To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
modeling pronunciation probabilities in the lexicon improves WER by 0.4% on average, and modeling silence probabilities in the lexicons improves WER by an additional 0.3% on average.

(1) pronunciation probabilities can improve the word error rate by 1.2% absolute on average, and (2) word-specific silence probabilities can improve the error rate by an additional 1% absolute, on average, over the baseline.

(a) modeling pronunciation probabilities and silence probabilities in speech decoding is a good idea; (b) it is important to model the probability of silence after each individual word, and (c) the probability of each individual word after silence is an important factor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
modeling word-dependent silence probabilities in the context of ASR decoding.
modeling the probability of a word appearing in silence, as opposed to modeling the probability that a word is followed by silence.
improving the accuracy of ASR systems by modeling pronunciation and silence probability in a way that is compatible with FST-based decoding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
modeling pronunciation and silence probability improves the performance of ASR by 2-5% WER reduction.
the improvements from modeling pronunciation probabilities are small but fairly consistent, and the improvement from modeling word-specific silence probabilities is small and dataset-dependent.
pronunciation probabilities improve recognition performance, but silence probabilities are not as useful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a novel way to incorporate silence probabilities into ASR decoding, and that this has a small but consistent WER improvement across datasets.
modeling pronunciation and silence probability in the context of FST-based decoding is a simple and effective way to improve WER, especially for small vocabulary speech recognition tasks.
the improvement is more significant in the case of Switchboard and Librispeech, and less significant in the case in Wall Street Journal and TED-LIUM.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is possible to encode pronunciation probabilities and silence probabilities in a lexicon (L)-based transducer, which is useful for decoding with a small L transducer, as is often the case for large-vocabulary speech recognition.
it is relatively straightforward to encode these probabilities in the L transducer, and this can be done without modifying the decoder.
modeling word-dependent silence probabilities is a simple and effective way to improve ASR performance.
